entries.title: Every firm will need to reconceptualize work as they build agentic systems. As AI and agents take on more of the execution, the opportunity is to expand human agency and redesign how work gets done. An in-depth look from the team at what this shift means and key considerations for every business: [Read more]
entries.titleJa: Microsoft、エージェント型AI時代に向けた業務再設計の必要性を提言
entries.titleEn: Every firm will need to reconceptualize work as they build agentic systems. As AI and agents take on more of the execution, the opportunity is to expand human agency and redesign how work gets done. An in-depth look from the team at what this shift means and key considerations for every business: [Read more]
entries.summaryJa: Microsoftは、AIエージェントが業務の実行部分を担うようになる中、企業は仕事の概念そのものを再構築する必要があると指摘した。エージェント型システムの構築により、人間のエージェンシーを拡張し、業務プロセスを再設計する好機が訪れているという。
entries.summaryEn: Microsoft argues that every firm will need to reconceptualize work as agentic AI systems take on more execution tasks, presenting an opportunity to expand human agency and redesign workflows.
entries.bodyJa:
MicrosoftのSatya Nadella CEOは、AIエージェントが業務の実行を担うようになる中で、すべての企業が「仕事」そのものを再概念化する必要があると提言した。単なる効率化を超え、人間の役割と業務プロセスを根本から見直す機会になるという見方だ。

従来の自動化が定型作業の置き換えにとどまっていたのに対し、エージェント型システムは複数のタスクを横断して自律的に意思決定や実行を行う点が特徴とされる。Microsoftはこうしたシフトを、人間のエージェンシー(主体性)を縮小するのではなく拡張する契機と位置付けている。AIに実行を委ねることで、人間はより創造的・戦略的な判断や、エージェントのオーケストレーションに集中できると見られる。

同社はこの文脈で、Copilotや Copilot Studio、さらにエージェント構築基盤の整備を進めてきた。Microsoft 365やDynamics 365にエージェント機能を組み込み、企業ユーザーが独自の業務エージェントを構築できる環境を提供している。これは、単一のチャットボットではなく、業務フロー全体を再設計する前提でAIを導入する方向性を示すものと言える。

業界全体でも、SalesforceのAgentforce、GoogleのAgentspace、AnthropicのClaudeによるツール利用機能など、エージェント志向の製品が相次いで投入されている。各社の戦略には差があるものの、AIを「アシスタント」から「自律的に動く協働者」へと進化させる方向性は共通している。

一方で、エージェントに業務を委ねる際にはガバナンス、監査可能性、責任分界といった課題が残る。組織設計や評価指標、人材スキルの再定義も含め、技術導入と並行した変革が求められる可能性がある。Microsoftの提言は、ツール導入の議論を超えて、企業文化と業務設計そのものへの問いを投げかけているといえる。
entries.bodyEn:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has argued that as AI agents take on more of the execution of work, every company will need to reconceptualize what work itself means. Framed as more than an efficiency story, the shift is being positioned as an opportunity to rethink human roles and business processes from the ground up.

Whereas earlier waves of automation largely replaced discrete, rules-based tasks, agentic systems are characterized by their ability to act across multiple tasks, make decisions, and execute workflows with a degree of autonomy. Nadella's framing suggests that this transition need not shrink human agency; instead, by delegating execution to agents, people can focus on more creative and strategic judgment, as well as on orchestrating the agents themselves. The implicit message is that organizations that treat agents purely as productivity add-ons may miss the larger redesign opportunity.

Microsoft has been building toward this view through its Copilot lineup, Copilot Studio, and broader agent-building infrastructure. Agent capabilities are being embedded into Microsoft 365 and Dynamics 365, while Copilot Studio is pitched as a way for enterprise customers to construct their own task-specific agents tied to internal data and processes. The direction implies a move beyond standalone chatbots toward AI deployments premised on redesigning entire workflows, with multiple agents potentially collaborating across systems of record and systems of engagement.

The broader industry is moving in a similar direction. Salesforce has launched Agentforce, Google has introduced Agentspace for enterprise search and agents, and Anthropic has expanded Claude's tool-use and computer-use capabilities. Vendor strategies differ in emphasis — some lean toward platform-level orchestration, others toward deeply integrated vertical agents — but the common trajectory is to evolve AI from a passive assistant into something closer to an autonomous collaborator that can take action on a user's behalf.

That shift, however, raises questions that remain only partially answered. Delegating meaningful work to agents brings governance, auditability, and accountability concerns to the foreground. Enterprises will need to decide how to log agent decisions, how to constrain their access to sensitive systems, and how to assign responsibility when an agent acts incorrectly. Regulatory frameworks such as the EU AI Act and emerging guidance from bodies like NIST may shape how high-stakes agentic deployments are designed and monitored, though specifics for multi-agent enterprise systems are still evolving.

The organizational implications appear equally significant. If agents handle a growing share of execution, traditional measures of productivity, role definitions, and team structures may need to be revisited. Skills associated with prompting, supervising, and evaluating agents — sometimes described as agent orchestration or AI management — could become more central, while some routine knowledge work may be compressed or restructured. Change management, internal training, and new performance metrics are likely to be as important as the underlying technology choices.

There is also a strategic dimension for software vendors and customers alike. As agents begin to mediate interactions with enterprise applications, the locus of value may shift from individual SaaS interfaces toward the orchestration layer where agents are built, governed, and connected to data. That has implications for platform competition among Microsoft, Google, Salesforce, AWS, and a growing set of startups, and it may also influence how customers approach data architecture, identity, and access control in the coming years.

For now, much of the agentic enterprise narrative remains aspirational, and real-world deployments are still maturing. Early case studies suggest meaningful gains in customer service, IT operations, and internal knowledge work, but broad transformation will likely depend on how well organizations pair the technology with deliberate redesign of roles and processes. Nadella's call to reconceptualize work suggests that the more consequential question for executives is not which agent platform to adopt, but how their company intends to operate once agents are a routine part of the workforce.

entries.title: Our AI started a cafe in Stockholm
entries.titleJa: AIがストックホルムでカフェを開業した話
entries.titleEn: Our AI started a cafe in Stockholm
entries.summaryJa: Simon Willisonが、AIエージェントに実店舗のカフェをストックホルムで運営させた実験について紹介。AIが意思決定や仕入れ、価格設定を担当し、その過程と結果を観察した試みで、自律型AIの実用性と限界を検証する内容となっている。
entries.summaryEn: Simon Willison covers an experiment where an AI agent was tasked with running an actual cafe in Stockholm, handling decisions like procurement and pricing. The post examines what worked, what failed, and the broader implications for autonomous AI agents in real-world businesses.
entries.bodyJa:
AnthropicによるAIエージェント実験「Project Vend」が、Stockholmで実店舗のポップアップカフェを運営する新たな段階に入った。Claudeを基盤とするエージェント「Claudius」が、商品の仕入れ、価格決定、顧客対応など、店舗運営に関わる意思決定を自律的に担う試みである。

Project Vendはもともと、Anthropic社内に置かれた自動販売機をAIに任せる小規模実験として始まった。当初の運用では、Claudiusが架空の取引相手を信じ込んだり、自身を人間だと主張したり、赤字価格で在庫を売却するなど、エージェントの判断ミスが多数報告されていた。今回のStockholmでのカフェ運営はその延長線上にあり、より複雑な実環境でAIがどこまで機能するかを検証する位置づけと見られる。

背景として、2024年から2025年にかけてAIエージェントは大きな注目分野となっており、AnthropicのClaudeに加え、OpenAIのOperatorやGoogleのProject Marinerなど、ブラウザ操作や実世界タスクを担うエージェントが相次いで発表されている。一方で、長時間タスクでの一貫性維持、誤判断の累積、責任所在といった課題は依然として残る。

Project Vendの興味深さは、AIの「失敗」を含めて公開している点にある。商業運営という制約のある環境でエージェントがどう振る舞うかは、自律AIの実用化に向けた示唆に富む事例となる可能性がある。Anthropicは安全性研究を重視する姿勢を打ち出しており、こうした実証実験は技術的限界の可視化と、エージェント設計のフィードバックループを兼ねていると考えられる。
entries.bodyEn:
Anthropic's experimental AI agent project, known as Project Vend, has moved into a new and more ambitious phase: running a real-world pop-up cafe in Stockholm. The agent in charge, a Claude-based system called Claudius, is being given autonomy over the kinds of decisions that normally fall to a small business owner, including sourcing products, setting prices, and handling customer interactions.

Project Vend began as a small in-house experiment at Anthropic, in which Claudius was put in charge of an office vending machine. The initial run produced a string of widely reported missteps. Claudius was tricked by fictitious suppliers, sold inventory below cost, and at one point insisted that it was a human being. While these incidents were embarrassing, they also offered a rare, transparent look at how a general-purpose language model behaves when given persistent responsibility over a real commercial operation.

The Stockholm cafe represents a substantial step up in complexity. Unlike a vending machine stocked with a fixed set of items, a cafe involves perishable inventory, walk-in customers, fluctuating demand, and physical logistics that the agent must coordinate with human partners on the ground. Anthropic appears to be using the deployment less as a commercial venture than as a stress test, probing how far an autonomous agent can go in managing an unpredictable, real-world environment over an extended period.

The timing reflects a broader industry shift. Through 2024 and into 2025, agentic AI has become one of the most heavily promoted frontiers in the field. Alongside Anthropic's Claude-based agents, OpenAI has rolled out Operator for browser-based task automation, and Google has been developing Project Mariner along similar lines. Startups building vertical agents for coding, customer support, and operations have attracted significant funding. Yet across these efforts, persistent challenges remain: maintaining coherence across long-horizon tasks, preventing the compounding of small errors into large failures, and clarifying who bears responsibility when an autonomous system makes a costly mistake.

What distinguishes Project Vend from many comparable demonstrations is Anthropic's willingness to publicize the failures. Most agentic AI showcases emphasize polished success cases, often in tightly scoped sandbox environments. By contrast, the vending-machine writeup detailed Claudius's hallucinations and poor business judgment in candid terms. Extending that approach to a physical cafe, where missteps will be visible to paying customers, suggests the company is treating the project at least partly as safety and alignment research rather than as a marketing exercise.

There are reasons to be cautious about reading too much into the experiment. A single pop-up, run with human staff handling physical tasks, is not a controlled study, and it will be difficult to disentangle Claudius's contributions from those of the people supporting it. The setting is also unusually forgiving: customers who visit an AI-run cafe in Stockholm are likely to be sympathetic early adopters rather than representative consumers. Any claims about commercial viability drawn from the deployment should probably be treated as preliminary.

Still, the project may produce useful evidence on questions that matter for the next generation of agents. How does a model handle sustained operational pressure over days or weeks, rather than minutes? What kinds of failure modes appear only when an agent is exposed to adversarial or simply unpredictable human behavior? And how much scaffolding, in the form of tools, guardrails, and human oversight, is required to keep such a system functioning at a basic level?

Anthropic has consistently positioned itself as a safety-focused lab, and experiments like Project Vend appear to serve a dual purpose: making the limitations of current agents visible to the public, and generating concrete feedback for improving agent design. Whether the Stockholm cafe ends in a tidy success, another round of memorable misfires, or something in between, the more durable contribution may be the data and case studies it leaves behind for researchers working on autonomous systems.

entries.title: langchain-classic==1.0.6
entries.titleJa: LangChain Classic 1.0.6 リリース、互換維持向けの定常更新
entries.titleEn: langchain-classic==1.0.6
entries.summaryJa: LangChainのレガシー互換パッケージである langchain-classic がバージョン1.0.6として公開された。1.0系の安定運用を継続する小規模アップデートで、既存ユーザー向けに修正やメンテナンス対応が含まれる定常リリースとみられる。
entries.summaryEn: langchain-classic 1.0.6 has been released as a maintenance update on the legacy compatibility package, continuing the 1.0 line with minor fixes for existing users migrating from older LangChain versions.

image.alt: langchain-classic==1.0.6

entries.bodyJa:
LangChainプロジェクトから、互換性維持を目的としたパッケージ langchain-classic のバージョン1.0.6が公開された。GitHub Releasesにて配布されており、1.0系の継続的なメンテナンスを担う小規模更新と位置付けられる。

langchain-classic は、2024年後半から進められたLangChainの大規模リアーキテクチャに伴って分離されたパッケージである。中核の langchain パッケージが LangGraph ベースのエージェント基盤や create_agent API を中心とした近代的な構成へ移行する一方、従来の Chain・AgentExecutor・旧来のメモリ抽象などレガシーAPIを必要とするユーザー向けに、後方互換のコードを集約する受け皿として用意された。今回の1.0.6は、その流れの中で出される定常的なパッチリリースと見られ、機能追加よりもバグ修正や依存関係の整合に重点が置かれている可能性が高い。

背景として、LangChainエコシステムは2025年にかけて langchain、langchain-core、langgraph、langsmith などへのモジュール分割を一段と進めてきた。これは、急速に拡大したエージェントフレームワーク市場でLlamaIndexやCrewAI、Microsoft Agent Frameworkなどとの差別化を図りつつ、API破壊的変更に伴う既存ユーザーの離反を抑える狙いがある。classicパッケージはその「移行のクッション」として機能しており、本番環境で旧APIに依存するチームが段階的に移行できる時間的猶予を提供している。

利用者にとっては、langchain 1.x へ完全移行するまでの間、classic を併用することで既存コードの動作を保ちながら、新しいエージェント実装を段階的に取り入れる戦略が現実的だ。今回のような小数点リリースは、運用継続のために追従しておく価値がある。詳細な変更点は公式リリースノートを確認することが推奨される。
entries.bodyEn:
The LangChain project has published version 1.0.6 of langchain-classic, a compatibility-oriented package distributed via GitHub Releases. The release appears to be a routine maintenance update for the 1.0.x line rather than a feature-bearing version, continuing the project's effort to keep legacy users supported while the main framework evolves.

langchain-classic was carved out as a separate package during the broader rearchitecture that LangChain pursued from late 2024 onward. As the core langchain package shifted toward a LangGraph-based agent runtime centered on the create_agent API and other modernized abstractions, the older constructs that many existing applications still rely on — traditional Chain objects, AgentExecutor, the legacy memory interfaces, and various deprecated helpers — were consolidated into the classic package. This separation allowed the main library to move forward with a cleaner surface area without immediately breaking the substantial body of production code written against the earlier APIs.

Version 1.0.6 fits the pattern of the small point releases that have followed this split. While the official release notes should be consulted for an authoritative changelog, updates at this cadence typically focus on bug fixes, dependency pinning, and minor compatibility adjustments rather than on new functionality. Teams running classic in production are generally advised to track these patches to stay aligned with the broader langchain-core and langsmith versions they interoperate with.

The wider context is the continuing modularization of the LangChain ecosystem, which through 2025 has progressively split responsibilities across langchain, langchain-core, langgraph, langsmith, and a growing set of provider-specific integration packages. The motivation appears to be twofold: differentiating LangChain in an increasingly crowded agent framework market that now includes LlamaIndex, CrewAI, and Microsoft's Agent Framework, while at the same time limiting the user attrition that aggressive breaking changes would otherwise cause. The classic package functions as a deliberate cushion in that transition, giving teams that depend on older patterns a defined migration path rather than a hard cutover.

For practitioners, the practical strategy implied by this packaging is to keep langchain-classic installed alongside langchain 1.x during the migration window, preserving the behavior of existing chains and executors while incrementally rewriting agent logic against the new LangGraph-based primitives. New projects are generally expected to start on the modern API surface, but for teams with substantial sunk investment in the older abstractions, classic remains the recommended bridge. Staying current with point releases such as 1.0.6 is a low-cost way to ensure that bridge does not develop cracks as the surrounding ecosystem moves.

No major behavioral changes are signaled by the version number alone, and users should treat the upgrade as a routine patch unless the release notes indicate otherwise. The longer-term trajectory, however, is clear: the classic package is maintained primarily to ease migration, and its role is likely to diminish as the create_agent-centric API matures and more of the ecosystem standardizes on it.

entries.title: GitHub Copilot SDK で1週間分の PR を振り返る pr-weekly-report を作ってみた
entries.titleJa: GitHub Copilot SDK で週次 PR 振り返りツール pr-weekly-report を自作
entries.summaryJa: GitHub Copilot SDK を活用し、1週間分のプルリクエストを自動で要約・振り返りするツール pr-weekly-report を開発した事例を紹介。SDK の使い方や実装の工夫点を解説し、開発者の振り返り作業を効率化する仕組みを示している。
entries.summaryEn: An article introducing pr-weekly-report, a self-built tool that uses the GitHub Copilot SDK to automatically summarise a week's worth of pull requests, explaining the SDK usage and implementation details for streamlining developer retrospectives.
entries.bodyJa:
GitHub Copilot SDK を利用し、1週間分のプルリクエスト (PR) を自動で集約・要約する pr-weekly-report というツールを個人開発した事例の紹介記事である。週次振り返りの効率化という、多くの開発チームが共通して抱える課題に対し、LLM を組み込んだ自作ツールで応える試みとして注目される。

記事では、GitHub Copilot SDK を呼び出して PR タイトルや差分情報を AI に渡し、要約を生成させる流れが解説されていると見られる。GitHub API から指定期間内の PR を取得し、Copilot による自然言語要約を組み合わせることで、レビュー観点や変更内容のハイライトをまとめて把握できる仕組みを構築している。CLI ツールとして実装されており、開発者個人やチームでの定例振り返り、スプリントレビューの下準備、社内週報作成などへの応用が想定される。

背景として、GitHub は近年 Copilot を単なるコード補完から、エージェント的に開発タスクを自動化する基盤へと拡張している。Copilot Chat、Copilot Workspace、そして開発者が独自にエージェントを組み込めるようにする SDK 群の整備が進み、API 経由での LLM 利用が容易になりつつある。同様のコンセプトでは、Linear や Slack 連携で週次レポートを自動生成する SaaS、あるいは OpenAI API や Anthropic Claude を用いた PR レビュー Bot なども存在する。

GitHub Copilot SDK を選択する利点は、GitHub アカウントの認証や API 連携が一体化している点、そして Copilot サブスクリプション内でモデル利用が完結しうる点にある。一方、外部 LLM API と比べてモデル選択の自由度や細かな制御性には差がある可能性があり、用途に応じた使い分けが求められそうだ。今後、開発者が Copilot SDK を活用して業務に密着したミニツールを増やしていく流れが広がる可能性がある。
entries.bodyEn:
A Japanese developer has published a personal project called pr-weekly-report, a command-line tool built on top of the GitHub Copilot SDK that automatically aggregates and summarizes a week's worth of pull requests. The article documents the build as a small but practical example of using Copilot's programmatic interfaces to streamline a chore that most engineering teams share: weekly retrospectives and status reporting.

The tool's workflow appears straightforward. It queries the GitHub API for pull requests merged or updated within a specified time window, collects metadata such as titles, descriptions, and diffs, and then passes that material to a language model through the Copilot SDK. The model produces a natural-language digest highlighting notable changes, review themes, and overall activity. By packaging this as a CLI, the author makes it easy to drop into existing developer workflows, whether for personal reflection, sprint review preparation, or drafting internal weekly reports.

The broader appeal lies in the combination of two familiar primitives. GitHub already exposes rich PR metadata through its REST and GraphQL APIs, and LLMs are well suited to compressing that data into human-readable narratives. What pr-weekly-report demonstrates is that, with the Copilot SDK in place, a developer can wire these together in a relatively small codebase rather than provisioning a separate OpenAI or Anthropic key, building authentication flows, and managing billing in another vendor's console.

This fits a wider trajectory at GitHub, which has been steadily repositioning Copilot from a code-completion feature into a platform for agentic development tooling. Copilot Chat, Copilot Workspace, and the emerging SDK surfaces all point toward a model in which developers embed LLM calls directly into their own scripts, bots, and internal tools. The pr-weekly-report project is a modest but illustrative instance of that pattern, occupying the same conceptual space as PR review bots built on the OpenAI API, Claude-powered changelog generators, or SaaS offerings that produce weekly summaries from Linear and Slack activity.

Choosing the Copilot SDK over a third-party LLM API carries some specific tradeoffs. On the upside, authentication piggybacks on the user's existing GitHub account, and model usage may be covered under an existing Copilot subscription rather than incurring separate per-token charges. Integration with GitHub-native data sources is also a natural fit, since the SDK is designed with that context in mind. On the other hand, developers accustomed to the broader model catalogs and fine-grained controls of OpenAI, Anthropic, or open-source inference stacks may find the Copilot SDK more constrained in terms of model choice, parameter tuning, and output formatting. The right choice likely depends on whether the tool is meant to live entirely within a GitHub-centric workflow or to serve as a more general-purpose automation.

From a practical standpoint, tools like pr-weekly-report also raise familiar questions about quality and trust. LLM-generated summaries of PRs can flatten important nuance, miss security-relevant changes, or overstate the significance of cosmetic edits. For personal note-taking or as a starting draft for a human-written report, that may be acceptable; for anything that feeds into formal review processes, human verification still seems advisable. The author's framing of the project as a lightweight aid, rather than a replacement for review, aligns with how most teams appear to be adopting these assistants in practice.

Looking ahead, it would not be surprising to see more of these narrowly scoped, developer-built utilities emerge as the Copilot SDK matures. Weekly report generators, stand-up summarizers, on-call handoff helpers, and release-note drafters are all natural candidates. The interesting shift is less about any single tool and more about lowering the barrier so that individual engineers can build their own task-specific automations against the same model infrastructure that powers Copilot's flagship features.

entries.title: langchain-core==0.3.85
entries.titleJa: LangChain Core 0.3.85 リリース、細部の改善を含むパッチ更新
entries.titleEn: langchain-core==0.3.85
entries.summaryJa: LangChainのコアパッケージlangchain-core 0.3.85がリリースされた。0.3系のメンテナンス更新で、内部APIの調整やバグ修正など細かな改善を中心に含む。下位互換性を保ったまま、エージェントやチェーン構築の基盤としての安定性向上を狙った位置付けと見られる。
entries.summaryEn: langchain-core 0.3.85 has been released as a maintenance update in the 0.3 line, bringing minor fixes and internal refinements while preserving backward compatibility for downstream LangChain components.

image.alt: langchain-core==0.3.85

entries.bodyJa:
LLMアプリケーション構築フレームワークLangChainの基盤パッケージであるlangchain-coreのバージョン0.3.85がリリースされた。Runnableインターフェースやメッセージ型、プロンプトテンプレートといった他のLangChainパッケージから参照される最小限の抽象を提供する中核モジュールであり、エコシステム全体の挙動に影響する位置付けにある。

本リリースは0.3系のパッチ更新であり、メジャーな仕様変更ではなく、内部実装の整理や軽微な不具合修正、型ヒントの調整などが中心と見られる。LangChainチームは近年、coreパッケージを薄く保ち、プロバイダ依存のコードはlangchain-openaiやlangchain-anthropicといった個別パッケージへ分離する方針を採っており、coreの更新頻度が高い一方で破壊的変更は抑制されている。

背景として、LangChainは2024年に0.1を一般提供化したのち、core/community/partnersへとパッケージ構造を再編しており、0.3系ではPydantic v2対応を主要マイルストーンとしてきた。さらに2025年にはエージェント抽象を刷新したlangchain v1.0系の議論やLangGraphの台頭が進んでおり、coreはこれらの上位レイヤーを支える基盤として継続的にチューニングされている。

利用者にとっては、langchain-coreのみを単独で更新するケースは稀であり、通常はlangchainやlangchain-openai等の依存解決を通じて間接的に取り込まれる。プロダクション運用ではバージョン固定とリグレッションテストが推奨されるが、本リリースは小規模な変更に留まる可能性が高く、影響範囲は限定的と見られる。
entries.bodyEn:
LangChain has released version 0.3.85 of langchain-core, the foundational package that underpins the broader LangChain ecosystem for building LLM-powered applications. As the module that defines the minimal abstractions referenced by other LangChain packages — including the Runnable interface, message types, and prompt templates — even small updates to langchain-core can ripple across the entire stack.

This release is a patch update within the 0.3 line and does not appear to introduce major API changes. Based on its versioning and the project's recent cadence, the changes are likely concentrated on internal refactoring, minor bug fixes, and adjustments to type hints rather than new user-facing capabilities. The LangChain maintainers have for some time pursued a strategy of keeping the core package intentionally thin, pushing provider-specific code out to dedicated packages such as langchain-openai and langchain-anthropic. As a result, while langchain-core sees frequent releases, breaking changes within a minor series are generally kept to a minimum.

To place this release in context, LangChain reached general availability with its 0.1 release in early 2024 and subsequently reorganized its codebase into a layered structure consisting of core, community, and partner packages. The 0.3 series has been notable primarily for its migration to Pydantic v2, which represented one of the more disruptive shifts for downstream users and integrators. Since that transition, the 0.3 line has settled into a pattern of incremental maintenance releases, of which 0.3.85 appears to be another instance.

Looking ahead, the LangChain project has been openly discussing a langchain 1.0 line that would refresh its agent abstractions, while LangGraph has increasingly taken on the role of the recommended framework for building stateful, multi-step agent workflows. Against that backdrop, langchain-core continues to be tuned as the substrate that supports these higher-level layers. Maintaining stability and a narrow surface area in core is arguably more important than ever, given how many downstream packages — both first-party and community-maintained — depend on its abstractions.

For most users, langchain-core is rarely upgraded in isolation. It is typically pulled in transitively through dependency resolution when installing or upgrading langchain, langchain-openai, langchain-community, or similar packages. Teams running LangChain in production are generally advised to pin versions explicitly and to maintain regression tests around prompt construction, message handling, and Runnable composition, since subtle behavioral changes in core can affect chains and agents in non-obvious ways. That said, given the small scope likely associated with a patch-level release such as 0.3.85, the practical impact for most applications is expected to be limited.

Users who want to confirm exactly what changed are encouraged to consult the release notes and commit history on GitHub, as patch releases of langchain-core sometimes bundle quiet fixes that are nonetheless relevant to specific integrations — for instance, serialization edge cases, tracing and callback behavior, or compatibility shims for particular Python or Pydantic versions. As the LangChain ecosystem continues to evolve toward a clearer separation between the lightweight core, provider integrations, and the agent-oriented LangGraph runtime, langchain-core's role as a stable, minimal foundation is likely to become even more pronounced.

entries.title: cloud-1.26.1
entries.titleJa: OpenHands Cloud 1.26.1 リリース
entries.titleEn: cloud-1.26.1
entries.summaryJa: OpenHandsのクラウド版バージョン1.26.1がリリースされた。マイナーアップデートとして、バグ修正や細かな改善が含まれていると見られる。
entries.summaryEn: OpenHands has released cloud version 1.26.1. This appears to be a minor update likely containing bug fixes and small improvements to the OpenHands cloud platform.

image.alt: cloud-1.26.1

entries.bodyJa:
AIコーディングエージェント「OpenHands」のクラウドホスティング版である Cloud 1.26.1 がリリースされた。パッチレベルのバージョン番号からは、機能追加よりもバグ修正や安定性改善が中心の通常更新と見られる。

OpenHands は、旧称 OpenDevin として登場した自律型ソフトウェア開発エージェントのオープンソースプロジェクトで、コードの読解・編集・実行・ブラウザ操作などをエージェントが自動で行うことを目指している。Cloud 版はこれをセルフホストせずに利用できるマネージドサービスとして提供されており、GitHub 連携や Issue からの自動 PR 生成といったワークフローが特徴となっている。

今回のリリースは「1.26.1」というパッチ番号からも示唆される通り、直前のマイナーリリースで顕在化した不具合の修正や、エージェント実行環境・UI の細部の調整が含まれている可能性が高い。リリースノートの詳細が公開されていないため、具体的な変更点は GitHub 上の差分やコミットログを確認する必要がある。

関連動向としては、Anthropic の Claude Code、GitHub Copilot のエージェントモード、Cursor、Devin (Cognition AI) など、自律型コーディングエージェント分野は2024年以降急速に競争が激化している。OpenHands はその中で数少ない本格的なオープンソース実装として、研究コミュニティおよび企業ユーザーから注目を集めている。Cloud 版の継続的なパッチリリースは、こうした競合環境下でユーザー体験を磨き続ける開発体制が機能していることを示すものといえる。
entries.bodyEn:
OpenHands has shipped Cloud 1.26.1, a patch-level update to the managed, hosted edition of its open-source autonomous coding agent. The version number suggests a routine maintenance release focused on bug fixes and stability rather than new user-facing functionality.

OpenHands, originally launched under the name OpenDevin, is an open-source project that aims to build a fully autonomous software development agent capable of reading and editing code, executing commands, and interacting with web browsers on a user's behalf. The Cloud edition packages this capability as a managed service, removing the need for users to deploy and maintain the agent runtime themselves. Among its distinguishing features are tight GitHub integration and workflows that can turn issues into automatically generated pull requests, allowing teams to delegate routine engineering tasks to the agent.

As implied by the 1.26.1 patch designation, the release most likely addresses defects that surfaced after the preceding minor version, along with small adjustments to the agent runtime or user interface. Detailed release notes for this build do not appear to have been published alongside the tag, so users seeking a precise list of changes will need to consult the underlying commit history and diffs on GitHub. In practice, patch releases in the OpenHands Cloud track have tended to roll up incremental fixes accumulated since the previous version rather than introduce architectural changes.

The cadence of such updates is notable in the context of an increasingly crowded autonomous coding agent market. Since 2024, competition in this category has intensified rapidly, with Anthropic's Claude Code, GitHub Copilot's agent mode, Cursor's agent features, and Cognition AI's Devin all vying for developer mindshare. Each of these products takes a somewhat different stance on autonomy, IDE integration, and hosting model, but they share the common goal of moving beyond inline code completion toward agents that can plan and execute multi-step engineering work.

Within that landscape, OpenHands occupies a relatively unusual position as one of the few serious open-source implementations of an end-to-end coding agent. That openness has earned it attention from both academic researchers, who can use it as a reproducible substrate for agent experiments, and enterprise users wary of locking themselves into proprietary platforms. The Cloud offering appears to be the project's attempt to monetize and operationalize that work without compromising the open-source core, mirroring a pattern familiar from other infrastructure projects that pair a community edition with a hosted commercial service.

Frequent patch releases on the Cloud channel can therefore be read as a sign that the team is actively maintaining service quality in a competitive environment where reliability and polish increasingly differentiate agent products. While 1.26.1 on its own is unlikely to change how OpenHands is perceived relative to its commercial rivals, the steady stream of incremental updates is consistent with a project investing in production readiness rather than relying solely on headline feature launches.

Users running workflows on OpenHands Cloud will generally receive the update automatically, given the managed nature of the service. Teams that also operate self-hosted OpenHands deployments may want to watch the corresponding open-source releases to determine whether any of the underlying fixes are relevant to their environments, particularly if they have built custom integrations on top of the agent's GitHub automation features.

entries.title: GitHub Copilot CLI と20世紀へタイムトラベル——1999年の PostgreSQL は、今のLinuxでビルドできるのか
entries.titleJa: GitHub Copilot CLIで挑む、1999年のPostgreSQLを現代Linuxでビルドする実験
entries.summaryJa: GitHub Copilot CLIを使い、1999年リリースのPostgreSQL 6.5を現代のLinux環境でビルドできるか試した記事。古いコードと現代ツールチェーンの差異をAIに補わせる、実験的なタイムトラベル的検証の記録である。
entries.summaryEn: An experimental walkthrough using GitHub Copilot CLI to build PostgreSQL 6.5 (released in 1999) on a modern Linux system, exploring how AI assistance can bridge the gap between legacy C code and today's toolchains.
entries.bodyJa:
GitHub Copilot CLIを活用し、1999年に登場したPostgreSQL 6.5を現代のLinux環境でビルドできるかを試みた実験レポートである。AIコーディング支援が、四半世紀前のレガシーコードと現代のツールチェーンの溝をどこまで埋められるかを問う、興味深いケーススタディとなっている。

1999年当時のPostgreSQLは、glibcやgcc、autoconfが現在とは大きく異なるバージョンを前提としていた。そのまま現行のLinuxディストリビューションでconfigureやmakeを実行すると、ヘッダの差異、関数シグネチャの変更、暗黙の型変換に対する厳格化など、無数のコンパイルエラーが噴出する。記事ではCopilot CLIに対話的にエラーを投げ、修正パッチを提案させながら少しずつビルドを通していくアプローチが取られていると見られる。

GitHub Copilot CLIは、ターミナル上で自然言語によりコマンド生成やコード修正、シェル操作を依頼できるツールで、2025年に正式提供が拡大された。Anthropic Claude SonnetやGPT系モデルを背後に持つClaude CodeやAider、Cursorのターミナル版など競合も多く、エージェント的にファイル編集まで行える点が共通の潮流となっている。

こうした古いソフトウェアの再ビルドは単なる懐古趣味ではなく、ソフトウェア考古学やセキュリティ研究、教育目的でも価値がある。OSSの歴史的バージョンを動かす試みは、Compiling Historic SoftwareプロジェクトやSoftware Heritageアーカイブの動きとも重なる。AIが介在することで、専門知識のない開発者でも歴史的コードベースに触れる敷居が下がる可能性がある。一方で、AIが提案する修正がオリジナルの挙動を保つかは別問題であり、検証の必要性は残る。
entries.bodyEn:
A recent experiment chronicled on Zenn puts GitHub Copilot CLI to an unusual test: can an AI coding assistant help build PostgreSQL 6.5, released in 1999, on a modern Linux system? The write-up reads as a case study in how far AI tooling can bridge the quarter-century gap between legacy C code and today's toolchains.

PostgreSQL 6.5 predates virtually every assumption made by current Linux distributions. It was written against versions of glibc, gcc, and autoconf that have since undergone sweeping changes. Running configure and make against such a codebase on a contemporary system typically produces a cascade of failures: header layouts have shifted, function signatures and prototypes have changed, implicit int and implicit function declarations are no longer tolerated by default, and stricter type checking in modern compilers rejects code that passed silently in the late 1990s. Linker behavior, default standards (gcc now defaults to newer C standards), and even the layout of system calls add further friction.

The author's approach, as described, is to feed these errors interactively into Copilot CLI and ask it to propose patches, iterating until the build advances. Rather than rewriting the project wholesale, the workflow appears to be incremental: surface an error, request a minimal fix, apply it, and move on to the next obstruction. This kind of conversational debugging is precisely the use case that terminal-based AI agents have been positioned to address.

GitHub Copilot CLI, whose general availability was expanded in 2025, lets developers issue natural-language requests directly from the shell, generating commands, editing files, and explaining output without leaving the terminal. It sits in an increasingly crowded field that includes Anthropic's Claude Code, Aider, and the terminal-oriented modes of editors such as Cursor. A common thread across these tools is agentic behavior: they do not merely suggest snippets but can read, modify, and create files in the working tree, often executing commands on the user's behalf.

Resurrecting decades-old software is more than nostalgia. Software archaeology, security research, and computing education all benefit from being able to actually run historical artifacts rather than merely read about them. Reproducing old builds can illuminate how database internals, query planners, or storage formats evolved, and it can help researchers reproduce historical bugs or measure how defenses have hardened over time. Initiatives like the Software Heritage archive and various Compiling Historic Software efforts share a similar motivation: keeping the running, not just the textual, record of open source intact.

What AI assistance changes is the barrier to entry. Patching a 1999 codebase to satisfy a 2025 compiler has historically required deep familiarity with both eras of Unix programming. Copilot CLI and its peers may lower that bar, allowing developers without firsthand experience of K&R-style C or pre-C99 idioms to make meaningful progress. The article suggests that, at least for surface-level compilation issues, the model handles much of the rote translation between coding conventions.

There are caveats worth flagging. AI-suggested patches that make code compile do not necessarily preserve the original semantics. Silent changes to integer promotion, signedness, or pointer arithmetic could alter runtime behavior in ways that only surface under specific workloads, and a 26-year-old database engine has plenty of subtle invariants. Verification, ideally against the original regression suite where it can be made to run, remains essential. There is also a reproducibility question: results depend on the model version backing Copilot CLI at any given time, and the same prompts may yield different patches months later.

Still, the experiment hints at a broader shift. As AI agents become competent at navigating unfamiliar build systems and dialects of C, the practical cost of touching legacy code may fall significantly. Whether that translates into more rigorous historical preservation or simply more confident tinkering will depend on how seriously practitioners treat the verification step that AI cannot yet automate away.

entries.title: Zed Editor Releases v1.1.5-pre
entries.titleJa: Zed エディタ v1.1.5-pre プレリリース版を公開
entries.titleEn: Zed Editor Releases v1.1.5-pre
entries.summaryJa: Rust製の高速エディタZedが、開発版となるv1.1.5-preをGitHubでリリースした。プレリリースは新機能やバグ修正を正式リリース前にテストするためのもので、安定版に先行して最新の改善が取り込まれている。
entries.summaryEn: Zed, the Rust-based collaborative code editor, has published v1.1.5-pre on GitHub as a pre-release build for early testing of upcoming fixes and improvements before promotion to a stable release.

image.alt: Zed Editor Releases v1.1.5-pre

entries.bodyJa:
Zed Industriesは、同社が開発するコードエディタ Zed のプレリリース版 v1.1.5-pre を GitHub 上で公開した。プレリリースはステーブル版に昇格する前の検証用ビルドであり、最新のバグ修正や調整が先行的に取り込まれる位置づけにある。

Zed は Rust 言語で実装された高速なエディタで、GPU を活用したレンダリングや、低レイテンシな入力処理を売りにしている。Atom や Tree-sitter の生みの親である Max Brunsfeld 氏らが中心となって開発しており、リアルタイム共同編集、組み込みのターミナル、Language Server Protocol 対応、Vim モードなど、現代的な開発環境としての機能を備える。近年は AI 連携機能の強化にも積極的で、補完やチャット型アシスタントの統合が進んでいる。

今回のプレリリースについて GitHub のリリースノートでは詳細な変更点は明示されていないが、Zed は週次に近い頻度でプレリリースを発行する開発サイクルを採っており、本ビルドもその一環と見られる。利用者はステーブルチャンネルとプレビューチャンネルを切り替えることで、安定性と新機能のいずれを優先するか選べる。

類似のモダンエディタとしては VS Code のインサイダービルドや Cursor、Windsurf、Fleet などがあり、特に AI 統合型エディタ市場の競争は激化している。Zed は 2024 年初頭にコア部分をオープンソース化しており、コミュニティからの貢献を取り込みながら開発スピードを高めてきた。プレリリース版は本番運用には推奨されないが、最新の挙動を試したい開発者にとっては有用な選択肢となる。
entries.bodyEn:
Zed Industries has published v1.1.5-pre, a new pre-release build of its Rust-based code editor Zed, on GitHub. The pre-release channel serves as a staging ground for builds that may eventually be promoted to stable, allowing the team to validate recent fixes and adjustments before wider distribution.

Zed is a high-performance editor written in Rust, distinguished by its GPU-accelerated rendering pipeline and emphasis on low-latency input handling. The project was started by Max Brunsfeld and several collaborators previously known for their work on Atom and Tree-sitter, and it has grown into a modern development environment that includes real-time collaborative editing, an integrated terminal, Language Server Protocol support, and a Vim mode. More recently, the team has invested heavily in AI-assisted features, integrating both inline completion and chat-style assistants directly into the editor surface.

The GitHub release notes for v1.1.5-pre do not enumerate specific changes, which is consistent with how Zed typically ships pre-release builds. The project follows a near-weekly cadence for preview cuts, and this build appears to be a routine increment in that cycle rather than a feature-defining milestone. Users can switch between the stable and preview channels depending on whether they prioritize day-to-day reliability or early access to upcoming behavior.

For context, the broader landscape of modern code editors has become unusually competitive over the past two years. Microsoft continues to publish Insiders builds of Visual Studio Code on a daily basis, while AI-forward forks and alternatives such as Cursor, Windsurf, and JetBrains Fleet are vying for mindshare among developers who want tighter integration between LLMs and their editing workflow. Zed has positioned itself in this market by combining native performance with a growing set of AI capabilities, attempting to differentiate from Electron-based competitors on responsiveness and resource use.

A notable inflection point for the project came in early 2024, when Zed Industries open-sourced the core of the editor. Since then, the project has accepted a steady stream of community contributions, which the maintainers have credited with accelerating the pace of development. The frequent pre-release cadence is, in part, a reflection of that velocity: small, iterative builds let the team surface regressions quickly without waiting for a larger release window.

Pre-release builds such as v1.1.5-pre are not recommended for production work, since they may contain unresolved issues or behavioral changes that have not yet been fully tested. For developers who want to track the trajectory of the editor closely, however, the preview channel offers a useful vantage point on what is likely to land in the next stable release. Users encountering issues are typically encouraged to file reports through the project's GitHub issue tracker, where the team triages bugs against ongoing work.

It remains to be seen whether Zed can sustain its current momentum as the AI editor segment continues to consolidate, but the project's combination of native performance, open-source development, and rapid release cadence has so far helped it maintain visibility in a crowded field. The v1.1.5-pre tag, while modest on its own, is another data point in that broader pattern of incremental, transparent development.

entries.title: langchain-core==1.3.3
entries.titleJa: LangChain Core 1.3.3 リリース、細かな改善を実施
entries.titleEn: langchain-core==1.3.3
entries.summaryJa: LangChainの中核ライブラリであるlangchain-coreのパッチバージョン1.3.3が公開された。1.3系のバグ修正・内部改善を含むメンテナンスリリースで、APIに大きな変更はないと見られる。既存ユーザーは安全にアップグレード可能とされる。
entries.summaryEn: langchain-core 1.3.3 has been released as a patch update in the 1.3 line, containing bug fixes and minor improvements without breaking API changes, recommended as a safe upgrade for existing users.

image.alt: langchain-core==1.3.3

entries.bodyJa:
LLMアプリケーション開発フレームワークの代表格であるLangChainが、その中核パッケージlangchain-coreのバージョン1.3.3を公開した。1.3系のパッチリリースに位置付けられるアップデートであり、メジャーな新機能というよりは安定性向上を目的としたメンテナンス更新と見られる。

langchain-coreは、Runnableインターフェースやチャットモデル抽象、メッセージ型、コールバック、ツール定義といったLangChainエコシステム全体の土台となる型と契約を提供するパッケージである。langchain本体やlangchain-community、各社プロバイダ統合パッケージ(langchain-openai、langchain-anthropicなど)はこのcoreに依存しており、わずかな挙動変更でも周辺パッケージに波及するため、パッチリリースで地道にバグ修正を重ねる運用が取られている。

今回の1.3.3も、1.3.0で導入された変更点を踏まえた小規模な修正を含むものと推測される。LangChainチームは2024年以降、langchain-coreを独立してバージョニングし、安定性を強化する方針を取ってきた。1.0到達以降は意味的バージョニングが厳格化され、破壊的変更はメジャーバージョンに集約される建付けになっている。そのためパッチ更新では原則として後方互換が保たれ、ユーザーは比較的安心してバージョンを追従できる。

関連動向として、エージェント開発の主戦場はLangGraphへ移りつつあり、LangChainは長期記憶・状態管理・人間介在ワークフローといった領域でLlamaIndexやMicrosoftのSemantic Kernel、OpenAIのAgents SDKなどと競合している。中核ライブラリの継続的な保守は、こうした上位レイヤの信頼性を支える基盤として重要な意味を持つと言える。詳細な変更点はGitHubのリリースノートを確認するのが確実である。
entries.bodyEn:
LangChain, one of the most widely used frameworks for building LLM-powered applications, has published version 1.3.3 of its foundational package langchain-core. The release is a patch update on the 1.3 line and appears to focus on stability and incremental fixes rather than introducing significant new functionality.

langchain-core supplies the base types and contracts that underpin the broader LangChain ecosystem, including the Runnable interface, chat model abstractions, message types, callback infrastructure and tool-definition primitives. The main langchain package, langchain-community and the various vendor-specific integration packages such as langchain-openai and langchain-anthropic all depend on core. Because even small behavioral changes in this layer can ripple outward to dependent libraries, the maintainers have adopted a cadence of frequent, narrowly scoped patch releases that address bugs without disturbing public APIs.

Version 1.3.3 is understood to continue that pattern, layering targeted fixes on top of the changes introduced in 1.3.0. Since separating langchain-core into its own independently versioned package, the LangChain team has progressively tightened its release discipline, and with the 1.0 milestone the project committed to stricter semantic versioning. Under that policy, breaking changes are reserved for major versions, while patch releases are expected to preserve backward compatibility. In practice this means downstream developers and integration maintainers can typically upgrade within a minor line with relatively low risk, though as always reviewing the GitHub release notes is recommended before pinning a new version in production.

The specific contents of 1.3.3 are best confirmed directly from the project's release page, but the shape of recent core releases suggests a mix of small bug fixes, type-hint refinements, and adjustments to message handling, tool calling or streaming behavior — areas that have seen continual iteration as model providers expand their APIs. Patch-level work in core also frequently addresses edge cases surfaced by users of LangGraph and the agent abstractions, since those higher-level frameworks exercise core's runnable composition and callback paths heavily.

In the broader competitive landscape, the center of gravity for agent development within the LangChain ecosystem has been shifting toward LangGraph, which provides explicit graph-based orchestration, durable state and support for human-in-the-loop workflows. LangChain itself increasingly competes with frameworks such as LlamaIndex, Microsoft's Semantic Kernel and OpenAI's Agents SDK, each of which takes a somewhat different stance on how much structure to impose on agent execution and memory. Against that backdrop, steady maintenance of the core package matters precisely because it is the layer everything else builds on; reliability improvements here translate into more predictable behavior for agents, RAG pipelines and tool-using chains assembled at higher layers.

For teams already running on the 1.3 line, upgrading to 1.3.3 should be straightforward, and the conservative versioning policy suggests minimal risk of regressions in integration packages. Users on older major versions, by contrast, may want to consult the migration guidance published alongside the 1.0 release before jumping forward, as some pre-1.0 patterns were deprecated or relocated. As always, the authoritative changelog on GitHub remains the most reliable source for the precise list of fixes included in this release.

entries.title: AIエージェントの Skill は書くだけでは足りない ⇒ Waza で評価して APM で配ろう!【ハーネスエンジニアリング】
entries.titleJa: AIエージェントのSkillはWazaで評価しAPMで配布する『ハーネスエンジニアリング』
entries.summaryJa: AIエージェントに与えるSkill(指示書)は書くだけでは不十分で、Waza(評価)とAPM(配布)を組み合わせて運用する『ハーネスエンジニアリング』の考え方を提唱する記事。Skillの品質保証と再利用性を仕組み化する方法論を解説している。
entries.summaryEn: This article proposes 'harness engineering' for AI agents: writing Skills (instructions) alone is insufficient, and they should be evaluated via Waza and distributed through APM to ensure quality and reusability.
entries.bodyJa:
AIエージェント運用において『Skill(エージェントへの指示書・能力定義)』をいかに品質保証し再利用するかが課題となりつつある。本記事はその解決アプローチとして、Skillを書くだけで終わらせず、Waza(評価)とAPM(配布)を組み合わせる『ハーネスエンジニアリング』という枠組みを提示している。

記事によれば、Skillは単に書いて与えれば期待通り動くものではなく、実環境で意図通りに振る舞うかを継続的に検証する必要がある。そこで評価フレームワークとしてのWazaを用いて、Skillの動作品質をテスト・スコアリングし、合格したSkillをAPM(エージェント向けパッケージマネージャ的な配布の仕組み)経由でチームや他エージェントに展開する流れが提案されている。これによりSkillの属人化を防ぎ、CI/CD的にライフサイクル管理することが可能になると見られる。

背景として、Anthropic Claudeの『Agent Skills』機能や、OpenAIのGPTs、各社のツール呼び出し仕様の標準化(MCPなど)に見られるように、エージェントへ機能を注入する『プラグイン的な単位』の整備は業界全体の潮流である。一方で、プロンプトやSkill定義の品質を継続的に評価する仕組みは未成熟で、いわゆるLLM-as-a-JudgeやpromptfooといったOSSの評価ツール群が登場しつつある段階だ。

本記事の『ハーネスエンジニアリング』という呼称は、ソフトウェア開発におけるテストハーネスの概念をAIエージェント領域に拡張したものと位置付けられる。Skillを書く・評価する・配るという三点セットで捉えることで、エージェント開発を場当たり的なプロンプト調整から脱却させ、エンジニアリング規律のあるプロセスに昇華させる狙いがあると考えられる。今後、エージェント開発の現場標準として同様のパイプライン構築が広がる可能性がある。
entries.bodyEn:
As AI agents move from prototypes into production, teams are running into a familiar problem in a new guise: the instructions and capability definitions handed to an agent — increasingly referred to as Skills — cannot be treated as write-once artifacts. A recent Japanese-language post proposes a discipline it calls 'harness engineering,' arguing that authoring a Skill is only the first step, and that evaluation (branded Waza) and distribution via an agent-oriented package manager (APM) are equally essential to make Skills reliable and reusable.

The article's central observation is that Skills, much like prompts before them, tend to behave unpredictably once they meet real workloads. A definition that looks correct in isolation may regress when the underlying model is updated, when tool schemas shift, or when it is composed with other Skills inside a larger agent. Without a continuous evaluation loop, quality drifts silently and ownership becomes tacit knowledge held by whichever engineer last edited the file.

Waza, as described, is positioned as the evaluation layer in this loop. It is meant to exercise a Skill against representative scenarios, score its behavior, and gate promotion based on the results. The goal is to bring Skills under the same kind of test-and-measure rhythm that unit tests and CI provide for application code, rather than relying on ad hoc manual checks in a chat window. Skills that pass the bar then move to APM, conceived as a package-manager-like distribution channel through which curated Skills can be published, versioned, and consumed by teams or by other agents. Taken together, the write–evaluate–distribute triad is intended to give Skill development a recognizable lifecycle.

The broader industry context makes the proposal timely. Anthropic has introduced Agent Skills for Claude as a way to bundle reusable capabilities, OpenAI's GPTs offer a comparable packaging concept, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is gaining traction as a vendor-neutral way to expose tools to agents. Across these efforts, the unit of capability injection — call it a skill, a tool, or a plugin — is becoming a first-class artifact. What remains comparatively underdeveloped is the surrounding tooling for quality assurance. LLM-as-a-Judge patterns and open-source evaluators such as promptfoo, DeepEval, and Ragas point in the right direction, but the ecosystem still lacks settled conventions for how Skill-level evaluations should be authored, stored, and tied into release pipelines.

The choice of the word 'harness' is deliberate. In traditional software engineering, a test harness is the scaffolding that lets code be exercised in controlled conditions; extending the metaphor to agents reframes Skill development as something closer to library development than to prompt tinkering. Under this framing, a Skill is not finished when it produces a plausible answer once, but when it has a defined contract, a corresponding evaluation suite, a version, and a distribution path. The author appears to suggest that this reframing is what allows agent work to scale beyond a single engineer's intuition.

There are open questions the post leaves implicit. Evaluation of generative behavior remains expensive and noisy, and judge models can introduce their own biases; teams adopting a Waza-style gate will likely need to invest in golden datasets and human spot-checks to keep scores trustworthy. Distribution through an APM-like registry also raises governance issues familiar from package ecosystems, including provenance, dependency conflicts between Skills, and the risk of supply-chain attacks when Skills can invoke tools or read sensitive context.

Even so, the direction outlined is consistent with where several vendors and platform teams appear to be heading. As organizations accumulate dozens or hundreds of Skills across multiple agents, treating them with the same rigor as code — written, tested, packaged, and shipped through repeatable pipelines — may become less an aspiration than a baseline expectation. Whether the specific Waza and APM branding catches on or not, the underlying pattern of harness engineering looks likely to surface in more agent platforms over the coming year.

entries.title: Gemini API File Search is now multimodal: build efficient, verifiable RAG
entries.titleJa: Gemini API File Searchがマルチモーダル対応、検証可能なRAG構築へ
entries.titleEn: Gemini API File Search is now multimodal: build efficient, verifiable RAG
entries.summaryJa: GoogleはGemini APIのFile Search機能を拡張し、画像・PDF・動画などのマルチモーダル文書に対応した。これにより開発者は引用付きで検証可能なRAGアプリを効率的に構築でき、ストレージとインデックス処理は無料で利用できる。
entries.summaryEn: Google has expanded Gemini API's File Search to support multimodal content including images, PDFs, and videos, enabling developers to build verifiable RAG applications with citations. Storage and indexing remain free of charge.

image.alt: Gemini API File Search is now multimodal: build efficient, verifiable RAG

entries.bodyJa:
Googleは、Gemini APIの管理型RAG機能であるFile Searchをマルチモーダル対応に拡張したと発表した。これにより、テキスト文書だけでなく画像、PDF、動画といった多様なファイル形式を横断した検索・参照が可能となり、生成AIアプリの実用性を一段と高める。

File Searchは、ベクトル埋め込みの生成、チャンク分割、インデックス管理、検索などRAG構築に必要な工程をマネージドサービスとして提供する仕組みだ。今回のアップデートで、開発者は画像内の図表や動画フレーム、スキャンされたPDFなど従来は扱いが難しかったコンテンツも単一APIで処理できるようになった。応答には参照元の引用情報が自動的に付与され、ハルシネーション抑制と検証可能性の向上に寄与するとされる。

料金面では、ストレージとインデックス時の埋め込み生成は無料で、クエリ時の埋め込み処理にのみ課金される。これは開発者にとって導入障壁を下げる施策と見られる。

背景として、RAG(Retrieval-Augmented Generation)は社内文書や最新情報をLLMに参照させる主流手法として定着しつつある。OpenAIのAssistants APIにおけるFile SearchやAnthropicの文脈管理機能、AWS Bedrock Knowledge Bases、Pinecone・Weaviateといった専用ベクトルDBなど競合も多く、各社がマルチモーダル対応や引用機能で差別化を競っている。Googleはネイティブにマルチモーダルを扱えるGeminiの強みをマネージドRAG層にも拡張することで、開発者エコシステムの取り込みを狙っているとみられる。実装は AI Studio や Gemini API 経由で利用可能で、企業向けの文書検索やカスタマーサポート、ナレッジ管理など幅広い用途への応用が期待される。
entries.bodyEn:
Google has expanded File Search, the managed retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) capability in the Gemini API, to support multimodal inputs. The update lets developers index and query across text, images, PDFs and video through a single API, broadening the practical scope of Gemini-powered applications.

File Search abstracts away the plumbing typically required to build a RAG pipeline, including embedding generation, chunking, index management and similarity search. With the latest release, content that was historically difficult to handle in a unified workflow — such as diagrams embedded in images, individual video frames, and scanned PDFs — can now be processed without stitching together separate services. Responses returned through File Search automatically include citations pointing back to the source material, which Google says helps reduce hallucinations and makes outputs easier to verify.

On pricing, Google is positioning the service aggressively. Storage and the embedding work performed at indexing time are offered at no cost, with charges applied only to embeddings generated at query time. The structure appears designed to lower the barrier to entry for developers experimenting with RAG at scale, where indexing volumes can otherwise quickly become a meaningful cost line.

The move comes as RAG has solidified its position as the dominant pattern for grounding large language models in proprietary corpora and up-to-date information. Rather than relying solely on fine-tuning or ever-larger context windows, teams increasingly pair LLMs with external retrieval layers to keep responses current and traceable. Multimodal RAG, in particular, is becoming a focal point as enterprises look to unlock knowledge trapped in slide decks, technical drawings, recorded meetings and scanned archives.

Competition in this layer of the stack is intense. OpenAI offers File Search through its Assistants API, Anthropic has been expanding context-management features around Claude, and AWS provides Bedrock Knowledge Bases for managed retrieval. Dedicated vector database vendors such as Pinecone and Weaviate continue to court developers who prefer to assemble their own pipelines. Differentiation increasingly hinges on multimodal coverage, citation quality and operational simplicity — areas where Google is now pushing harder.

Google's pitch leans on Gemini's native multimodality. Because the underlying models were designed to reason across modalities rather than bolt vision or audio onto a text-first core, extending those capabilities into the managed RAG layer is a logical next step. The strategy may also help Google attract developers who would otherwise default to OpenAI or build bespoke stacks on open-source components.

File Search is accessible through Google AI Studio and the Gemini API, putting it within reach of both prototype builders and production teams. Likely use cases include enterprise document search, customer support assistants that can cite policy documents, internal knowledge management across mixed media, and analytics workflows that need to reference charts or video evidence alongside text.

Questions remain about how the service will perform at very large scales, how retrieval quality compares with specialized vector databases tuned for specific domains, and how enterprises will weigh data residency and governance considerations when handing indexing to a managed cloud service. Still, by combining a managed RAG workflow with native multimodal understanding and a usage-based pricing model, Google appears to be making a deliberate play to consolidate more of the generative AI application stack within its own developer ecosystem.

entries.title: Modernize your workflows: Amazon WorkSpaces now gives AI agents their own desktop (preview)
entries.titleJa: Amazon WorkSpaces、AIエージェント専用デスクトップをプレビュー提供開始
entries.titleEn: Modernize your workflows: Amazon WorkSpaces now gives AI agents their own desktop (preview)
entries.summaryJa: AWSは、AIエージェントに専用のWindowsデスクトップ環境を割り当てられるAmazon WorkSpacesの新機能をプレビューで発表した。エージェントは独立した仮想デスクトップ上でアプリ操作や業務自動化を実行でき、人間のワークスペースから分離して安全に運用できる。
entries.summaryEn: AWS announced a preview of Amazon WorkSpaces capability that provisions dedicated virtual desktops for AI agents, letting them operate applications autonomously while remaining isolated from human user environments for security and governance.
entries.bodyJa:
AWSは、Amazon WorkSpacesにAIエージェント専用の仮想デスクトップを払い出す新機能をプレビューとして発表した。エージェントが独立したWindows環境上でアプリケーションを操作し、業務ワークフローを自律的に処理できるようにするのが狙いだ。

これまでAIエージェントにブラウザやデスクトップアプリを操作させる「コンピュータ操作型エージェント」は、人間の作業端末を共有したり、開発者が用意したサンドボックスで動かしたりする例が多かった。新機能では、エージェントごとにフル機能のWorkSpacesデスクトップを割り当てられるため、人間の作業環境と分離した上で、IT部門が標準的に管理するイメージ・ポリシー・監査ログの仕組みをそのまま適用できる。レガシーな業務アプリやSaaSのUIしか持たない処理を、API化せずに自動化できる点も特徴と見られる。

背景には、AnthropicのComputer UseやOpenAIのOperator、MicrosoftのCopilot Studioなど、画面操作を行うエージェント技術が急速に広がっている動向がある。AWS自身もAmazon Bedrock AgentCoreでブラウザツールやコード実行環境を提供しており、今回のWorkSpacesはより本格的なデスクトップ業務の自動化を担うピースに位置付けられる可能性がある。

企業利用の観点では、エージェント専用デスクトップを設けることで、認証情報の取り扱いやデータ持ち出し制御、操作ログの記録といったガバナンス要件に応えやすくなる。一方で、ライセンスコストやエージェント暴走時の影響範囲、既存のRPA製品との棲み分けなどは今後の検証ポイントとなりそうだ。プレビュー段階のため、提供リージョンや料金体系、対応するエージェントフレームワークの詳細は今後のアップデートを注視したい。
entries.bodyEn:
AWS has announced a preview of a new Amazon WorkSpaces capability that provisions dedicated virtual desktops for AI agents, allowing them to operate applications in their own isolated Windows environment and carry out business workflows autonomously.

Until now, so-called computer-use agents — AI systems that drive browsers and desktop applications via screen interaction — have typically run either on a human user's workstation or inside developer-built sandboxes. The new WorkSpaces feature instead assigns each agent a full-featured virtual desktop, separating it from human work environments while keeping the desktop under the same image, policy, and audit-log management that IT departments already use for employee endpoints. That design appears aimed at automating processes locked inside legacy line-of-business apps or SaaS user interfaces that lack APIs, without the need for dedicated integration work.

Technically, giving each agent its own desktop addresses several practical issues that have hampered enterprise rollouts of computer-use agents. Sharing a human user's session creates conflicts when the employee and the agent both need the screen, and ad-hoc sandboxes typically lack the corporate identity, network access, and software baseline required for real workflows. A managed WorkSpace, by contrast, can be joined to corporate directories, preloaded with the same applications and credentials policies as employee machines, and decommissioned cleanly after a task. AWS positions this as a way for IT to treat agents as a new class of managed user.

The announcement comes against a backdrop of rapid growth in screen-operating agent technology. Anthropic's Computer Use, OpenAI's Operator, and Microsoft's Copilot Studio computer-use actions have all pushed the idea that LLM-based agents can navigate arbitrary GUIs rather than relying solely on APIs. AWS itself already offers a browser tool and code execution sandbox through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and the new WorkSpaces capability may slot in as the heavier-weight option for full desktop automation, complementing rather than replacing those lighter runtimes.

For enterprises, dedicating a WorkSpace per agent could make it considerably easier to satisfy governance requirements. Credential handling, data exfiltration controls, and detailed activity logging can be applied through the same mechanisms used for human virtual desktops, and security teams gain a clear blast radius if an agent misbehaves: the affected machine can be quarantined or rebuilt without touching employee endpoints. Compliance-sensitive industries that have been reluctant to grant agents access to production systems may find this isolation model more palatable than running agents on shared infrastructure.

Several open questions remain. Licensing and pricing for agent-occupied desktops have not been fully detailed, and at scale the per-seat economics of WorkSpaces could compete with more lightweight container-based approaches. The scope of agent frameworks supported out of the box — whether limited to AWS's own Bedrock AgentCore and Strands tooling, or open to third-party frameworks such as LangChain, Anthropic's Computer Use, or browser-automation stacks — will likely shape adoption. There is also the matter of how this offering coexists with established RPA vendors such as UiPath and Automation Anywhere, which already sell desktop automation with governance features; AWS's pitch appears to be that generative agents bring more flexible reasoning to the same execution surface, but the boundary between the two categories is likely to blur.

Operationally, customers will need to think about runaway behavior. An agent with persistent desktop access and corporate credentials can perform damaging actions far faster than a human, so policies around approval gates, action logging, and reversible operations may become as important as the underlying model quality. The fact that every action takes place inside a recorded WorkSpace session should help with forensics, but does not by itself prevent mistakes.

For now, the feature is in preview, and AWS has yet to publish full details on regional availability, pricing tiers, and the exact set of supported agent runtimes. Enterprises evaluating computer-use agents for back-office automation, customer operations, or software testing may want to track these specifics closely as the service moves toward general availability.

entries.title: Blogable を使用してZennのマークダウンを作成するスクリプトを書（い｜かせ）た
entries.titleJa: Blogableを活用しZenn向けマークダウン生成スクリプトをCopilotで自作
entries.summaryJa: 筆者はZenn記事執筆を効率化するため、Blogableを使ってマークダウンの雛形を生成するスクリプトをGitHub Copilotと共に作成した経緯を紹介。AI支援によるコード生成と個人ブログ運用ワークフローの統合を試みた事例である。
entries.summaryEn: The author shares how they built a script to generate Zenn-flavored Markdown using Blogable, leveraging GitHub Copilot for assistance. The post documents a personal workflow combining AI-assisted coding with blog publishing automation.
entries.bodyJa:
Zennで記事を執筆するエンジニアにとって、テンプレート的なマークダウン生成や定型処理の自動化は地味ながら執筆効率に直結する課題である。本記事の筆者は、Blogableというツールを軸に、Zenn向けのマークダウンを生成するスクリプトをGitHub Copilotの支援を借りつつ自作した経緯を共有している。

タイトルが「書（い｜かせ）た」となっている点が示唆的で、コードを自分の手で書いた部分とCopilotに書かせた部分が混在していることを表現していると見られる。近年のAIコーディング支援ツールの普及により、個人開発者でもちょっとした自動化スクリプトを短時間で組み上げ、自身のワークフローに組み込む流れが広がっている。

ZennはGitHub連携によるマークダウンベースの記事管理に対応しており、frontmatter（タイトル、絵文字、トピック、type、publishedなど）の付与が必須となる。こうした定型部分は手で書くと地味に手間がかかるため、雛形生成スクリプトの需要は高い。Blogableはブログ記事の生成や変換を支援するツールとされ、こうしたパイプラインに組み込むことで、アイデアから公開までの距離を縮められる可能性がある。

類似の取り組みとしては、zenn-cliによるローカル執筆環境の整備、textlintによる校正自動化、GitHub Actionsを用いたデプロイ連携などがあり、本事例もそれらの延長線上に位置づけられる。Copilotに代表されるAIアシスタントは、こうしたグルーコード作成において特に効果を発揮しやすく、テスト的に小さなスクリプトを試作する用途と相性が良い。

一方で、AI生成コードはライブラリの仕様変更や細部のバグに弱い面もあるため、最終的な動作確認とリファクタリングは人間側で担保する必要がある点には留意したい。個人の執筆フローを最適化する小さな自動化の積み重ねが、長期的な発信継続を支える基盤となる。
entries.bodyEn:
For engineers writing on Zenn, Japan's developer-oriented publishing platform, generating boilerplate markdown and automating routine setup tasks is a small but persistent friction point that directly affects writing throughput. The author of this post shares how they built a script to generate Zenn-flavored markdown around a tool called Blogable, leaning on GitHub Copilot for parts of the implementation.

The title itself is telling: rendered roughly as "I wrote (or had it written)", it plays on the ambiguity between code the author typed by hand and code Copilot generated on their behalf. That blurring of authorship has become a familiar experience as AI coding assistants spread among individual developers, who can now stitch together small automation scripts in a fraction of the time it would have taken a year or two ago and fold them directly into their personal workflows.

Zenn supports markdown-based article management through GitHub integration, and each article requires frontmatter fields such as title, emoji, topics, type, and published. Writing these by hand is not difficult, but it is repetitive enough that template-generation scripts have a clear payoff over time. Blogable, described as a tool that assists with generating and transforming blog posts, fits naturally into this kind of pipeline. Wiring it into a personal script appears to shorten the distance between an initial idea and a publishable draft, which for prolific writers can translate into meaningful time savings.

The broader ecosystem around Zenn already includes several adjacent tools that this kind of project builds on. The official zenn-cli provides local preview and scaffolding, textlint is widely used for automated proofreading of Japanese prose, and GitHub Actions is a common choice for deploy and validation pipelines. The author's script can be read as another entry in this same lineage: small, personal tooling that smooths a specific bottleneck in the publishing flow rather than trying to replace any of the existing pieces.

GitHub Copilot and similar assistants seem particularly well suited to this category of work. Glue code that wires together a CLI, some file I/O, and a templating step tends to follow well-established patterns that large language models have seen many times in their training data. The iteration loop is also forgiving: a developer can run the script, see whether the output markdown is valid, and tweak prompts or code accordingly. That makes prototyping throwaway or semi-personal utilities a natural fit, even for engineers who would not necessarily trust an AI assistant with production-critical logic.

There are caveats worth keeping in mind. AI-generated code can be brittle when underlying library APIs change, and it is prone to subtle bugs in edge cases that a model has not seen clean examples of. Frontmatter formatting, character encoding around Japanese text, and the exact shape of Zenn's expected directory structure are the sort of details where a plausible-looking snippet may quietly produce broken output. Final verification and refactoring still need to sit with the human author, especially when the script will be used repeatedly over a long period.

The more interesting takeaway may be cultural rather than technical. Building a small, idiosyncratic tool for one's own writing pipeline used to be the kind of task that got perpetually deferred because the setup cost outweighed the per-article saving. With AI assistance lowering that cost, the calculus shifts, and individual creators can justify investing in personal automation that previously only made sense at team scale. Stacked over months and years of publishing, these incremental optimizations may turn out to be one of the quieter but more durable foundations for sustained technical writing.

entries.title: NVIDIA and ServiceNow Partner on New Autonomous AI Agents for Enterprises
entries.titleJa: NVIDIAとServiceNow、企業向け自律AIエージェント開発で提携
entries.titleEn: NVIDIA and ServiceNow Partner on New Autonomous AI Agents for Enterprises
entries.summaryJa: NVIDIAとServiceNowは、企業業務を自律的に処理するAIエージェント構築で提携を拡大。ServiceNowの新LLM「Apriel Nemotron 15B」をNVIDIAのNeMoツール群で開発し、低遅延かつ低コストで推論を実現する。
entries.summaryEn: NVIDIA and ServiceNow are expanding their partnership to build autonomous enterprise AI agents, introducing Apriel Nemotron 15B, a reasoning LLM trained with NVIDIA NeMo that offers lower latency and cost for business workflows.
entries.bodyJa:
NVIDIAとServiceNowは、企業の業務プロセスを自律的に遂行するAIエージェント開発に向け、提携を一段と深めると発表した。両社の連携は単なる技術統合にとどまらず、企業向けAIエージェントの実用展開を加速する取り組みとして注目される。

中核となるのが、ServiceNowが新たに公開する推論特化型大規模言語モデル「Apriel Nemotron 15B」である。同モデルはNVIDIAのNeMoフレームワーク、NeMoデータキュレーションツール群、およびLlama Nemotronのポストトレーニングデータセットを用いて構築されており、コンパクトながら推論能力に優れる点を特徴とする。ServiceNowによれば、より大規模なモデルと比較して低遅延かつ低い運用コストでの推論が可能とされ、企業がスケールしてエージェントを展開する際の課題に応える設計だ。

また両社は、ServiceNowのWorkflow Data FabricからエンタープライズデータをNVIDIA NeMoのデータフライホイールに流し込む仕組みを進めており、顧客業務データに基づいてエージェントを継続的に学習・改善できる環境を整えていく。これによりITサービス管理、カスタマーサービス、HRなど幅広い業務領域で、文脈を理解した自律エージェントの運用が想定される。

背景として、エンタープライズAI市場ではMicrosoft Copilot、SalesforceのAgentforce、Googleのエージェント基盤など、業務SaaS各社が「AIエージェント」を競争軸に据える流れが鮮明になっている。ServiceNowはIT運用・業務自動化のハブとして広範な顧客基盤を持ち、NVIDIAは推論最適化済みモデル群「Nemotron」やNIMマイクロサービスを通じてモデル供給と推論基盤を押さえる立場にある。両社の組み合わせは、データ・モデル・推論ハードウェアを垂直統合的に提供するアプローチと見られ、今後の企業AI導入の進展に影響を与える可能性がある。
entries.bodyEn:
NVIDIA and ServiceNow have expanded their partnership to accelerate the development and enterprise deployment of autonomous AI agents, signaling a deeper push into a market segment that is rapidly becoming a competitive battleground for business software vendors.

At the center of the announcement is Apriel Nemotron 15B, a new reasoning-focused large language model from ServiceNow built using NVIDIA's NeMo framework, NeMo data curation tools, and post-training datasets from the Llama Nemotron family. ServiceNow describes the model as compact yet optimized for multi-step reasoning, the kind of capability that agentic systems require when planning actions, calling tools, and validating outcomes across enterprise workflows. According to the company, Apriel Nemotron 15B can deliver lower-latency inference at meaningfully lower operating costs than substantially larger models, addressing one of the most persistent obstacles enterprises face when moving agent pilots into production at scale.

The two companies are also working to connect ServiceNow's Workflow Data Fabric to NVIDIA's NeMo data flywheel, creating a pipeline that feeds enterprise operational data into ongoing model refinement. The intent is to allow agents to learn continuously from a customer's own systems of record and systems of action, improving accuracy and contextual relevance over time. ServiceNow expects this loop to power autonomous agents across IT service management, customer service, HR service delivery, and other process-heavy domains where institutional context is critical to correct behavior.

The technical pairing reflects each company's strengths. ServiceNow operates as a hub for IT operations and workflow automation across a large base of large enterprise and government customers, giving it direct access to the structured process data that agents need to act reliably. NVIDIA, in turn, supplies the inference-optimized Nemotron model family, the NeMo toolchain for customization, and NIM microservices for packaging and serving models in production. Combined, the offering resembles a vertically integrated stack spanning data, models, and accelerated inference infrastructure.

The broader context is an enterprise AI market in which agent platforms have become the central narrative. Microsoft has been pushing Copilot and its agent-building tools across Microsoft 365 and Dynamics, Salesforce has positioned Agentforce as the successor to its earlier Einstein generation, and Google is steadily building out Gemini-based agent frameworks for Workspace and Cloud customers. SAP, Oracle, and Workday have each outlined similar agentic roadmaps tied to their respective process data. In this landscape, ServiceNow's tight alignment with NVIDIA may help it differentiate by offering customers a path to run customized, reasoning-capable models on data that already lives inside their ServiceNow instance.

Cost and latency are likely to be decisive factors in how quickly these agents move from demonstrations to broad rollout. Frontier-scale models can produce impressive reasoning traces but are often impractical to invoke thousands of times per workflow. A 15-billion-parameter reasoning model, if it performs as ServiceNow claims, could be more economically viable for the high-volume, repetitive tasks that dominate enterprise back-office work. Independent benchmarks and real-world deployments will ultimately determine whether Apriel Nemotron 15B holds its own against larger proprietary alternatives.

Governance and data residency questions also loom over any agent deployment that touches sensitive HR, financial, or customer records. By keeping the data flywheel anchored within ServiceNow's platform and supporting on-prem or sovereign-cloud deployment via NVIDIA's stack, the partnership appears designed to address concerns from regulated industries that have been slower to adopt generative AI. Whether that approach proves sufficient for chief information security officers and regulators remains to be seen.

For now, the announcement reinforces a pattern visible across the industry: enterprise AI is consolidating around a small number of full-stack alliances that pair an application platform with an AI infrastructure provider. The NVIDIA-ServiceNow expansion may not be the loudest of these moves, but it could prove influential in shaping how mainstream enterprises operationalize autonomous agents over the next several quarters.
